narratives.name: Deployment Maturity Journey
narratives.description: Application deployment progression on OpenShift

narrativeContexts.context: Application deployment on OpenShift progresses from manual GUI operations through CLI scripting to fully automated GitOps workflows with AI-assisted self-service capabilities provided by Developer Hub and OpenShift Lightspeed.

Begin with web console deployment to understand OpenShift fundamentals including pods, deployments, and services; adopt CLI for repeatability and version control; integrate pipelines for automation with testing and security scanning; mature to Developer Hub templates with built-in security guardrails and AI assistance.

Skipping CLI proficiency before automation leads to troubleshooting difficulties; neglecting pipeline testing causes production failures; failing to track developer experience metrics prevents optimization.

narratives.name: Scalability Maturity
narratives.description: Application scalability progression on OpenShift

narrativeContexts.context: Application scalability on OpenShift evolves from manual replica adjustment through policy-based automation to predictive optimization with cost awareness using HorizontalPodAutoscalers, ClusterAutoscaler, and ClusterResourceOverride operators.

Define resource requests and limits first to enable proper scheduling; implement HorizontalPodAutoscaler with appropriate metrics (CPU, memory, or custom); enable ClusterAutoscaler for elastic node capacity; mature to predictive analytics for proactive optimization based on historical patterns.

Setting resource requests far below actual usage causes constant scaling to maximum replicas; overly aggressive scaling policies cause replica count flapping; neglecting Pod Disruption Budgets risks availability during scale-down operations.

narrativeContexts.context: Application resilience on OpenShift matures from basic health probes through graceful degradation patterns to comprehensive SRE practices with error budget tracking and chaos engineering validation.

Implement liveness and readiness probes first with appropriate timeouts; add circuit breakers, retry logic, and graceful termination; centralize observability signals (logs, metrics, traces); adopt SRE practices with SLIs, SLOs, error budgets, and toil reduction.

Using same probe for liveness and readiness causes cascading failures during high load; missing timeout configurations allows request queueing; cause-based alerting generates excessive noise without actionable insights; neglecting error budgets prevents data-driven reliability decisions.

activities.name: Deploy Application from Source
activities.description: Deploy containerized application using Source-to-Image builds.

narratives.name: Deployment Technique
narratives.description: How to deploy applications using Source-to-Image

narrativeContexts.context: Source-to-Image builds create container images directly from source code without requiring Dockerfiles, supporting languages like Java, Node.js, Python, and Ruby.
Use web console to select source repository and builder image; configure environment variables and resource limits; trigger builds on Git push events; monitor build logs and deployment status.
Missing .s2i/environment file causes build failures; incorrect builder image selection leads to dependency errors; insufficient memory limits cause build pod evictions.

citationNames: Foundations of OpenShift

activities.name: Configure Application Health Probes
activities.description: Implement liveness, readiness, and startup probes for resilience.

narratives.name: Health Probe Configuration
narratives.description: How to configure health probes for resilience

narrativeContexts.context: Kubernetes provides three probe types: liveness (restart unhealthy pods), readiness (remove from service endpoints), and startup (delay other probes during initialization).

Implement health check endpoints in application code; configure liveness probe with appropriate timeout for restart; configure readiness probe to detect dependency failures; use startup probe for slow-starting applications; tune probe timing based on application behavior.
Using same endpoint for liveness and readiness causes cascading failures; overly aggressive probe timing causes restart loops; missing startup probe delays application readiness.

citationNames: 14 Best Practices for Developing Applications on OpenShift

activities.name: Implement Network Policies
activities.description: Define NetworkPolicy resources for pod-to-pod traffic segmentation.

narratives.name: Network Policy Implementation
narratives.description: How to implement network segmentation policies

narrativeContexts.context: NetworkPolicy resources restrict pod-to-pod traffic using label selectors, enabling zero-trust network segmentation within OpenShift clusters.

Start with deny-by-default policy blocking all ingress; define explicit allow rules for required communication paths; use label selectors for dynamic policy enforcement; implement egress policies to control outbound traffic; test policies in non-production before applying to production.
Missing default-deny policy leaves applications vulnerable; overly permissive rules negate security benefits; testing only ingress without egress leaves data exfiltration risks.

narratives.name: Autoscaling Configuration
narratives.description: How to configure horizontal pod autoscaling

narrativeContexts.context: HorizontalPodAutoscaler automatically adjusts replica counts based on observed CPU, memory, or custom metrics, ensuring applications scale elastically with demand.

Define resource requests and limits first; create HPA resource targeting desired CPU or memory utilization; configure min and max replica counts; define Pod Disruption Budgets to protect availability; monitor scaling events and tune thresholds based on application behavior.
Missing resource requests prevents HPA from calculating utilization; overly aggressive thresholds cause replica flapping; neglecting Pod Disruption Budgets risks availability during scale-down.

activities.name: Integrate CI/CD Pipeline Automation
activities.description: Configure Tekton pipelines with automated build, test, scan, and GitOps deploy stages.

narratives.name: CI/CD Pipeline Automation
narratives.description: How to integrate CI/CD pipeline automation

narrativeContexts.context: OpenShift Pipelines (Tekton) and OpenShift GitOps (Argo CD) provide cloud-native CI/CD automation, enabling pull-request-triggered workflows that build, test, scan, and deploy applications through declarative pipelines.

Define Tekton Pipeline resources with sequential tasks for checkout, build, test, and deploy; integrate vulnerability scanning as a quality gate; configure Argo CD Applications to sync from GitOps repository; set up automated sync policies with drift detection and rollback capability.

Monolithic pipelines with all stages in one task prevent granular debugging; missing quality gates allow broken builds to deploy; skipping automated testing in favor of manual verification creates deployment bottlenecks.

narratives.description: How to provision self-service development templates

narrativeContexts.context: Developer Hub software templates provide golden paths that codify organizational best practices, security guardrails, and deployment patterns into self-service application scaffolding.

Author Backstage template definitions with parameterized inputs and validation; embed security controls (SCC restrictions, network policies, resource limits) as non-optional template components; integrate with Argo CD for GitOps-first provisioning; connect OpenShift Lightspeed for AI-assisted debugging and recommendations.

Templates that are too restrictive discourage adoption; templates without security guardrails create a false sense of safety; failing to version templates leads to configuration drift across deployed applications.

activities.description: Define resource requests and limits and perform manual replica adjustment via console or CLI.

narratives.name: Manual Scaling Technique
narratives.description: How to configure manual application scaling

narrativeContexts.context: Manual scaling establishes the foundation for application scaling by defining resource requests and limits, and adjusting replica counts through the web console or oc scale command.

Define CPU and memory requests based on application profiling; set resource limits to prevent noisy-neighbor effects; use oc scale to adjust replica counts; verify load balancing distributes traffic across replicas; monitor resource utilization through console metrics.

Omitting resource requests causes scheduler to make poor placement decisions; setting limits too low causes OOMKilled pod restarts; scaling without verifying application statelessness causes data inconsistency.

activities.name: Implement Cluster Autoscaling
activities.description: Configure ClusterAutoscaler and MachineAutoscaler for elastic node capacity management.

narratives.name: Cluster Autoscaling Setup
narratives.description: How to implement cluster autoscaling

narrativeContexts.context: ClusterAutoscaler and MachineAutoscaler automatically adjust node capacity when pods cannot be scheduled, distributing across availability zones with configurable scaling rate limits.

Configure MachineAutoscaler with min/max replica counts per MachineSet; enable ClusterAutoscaler with scaling rate limits (25-50 machines at once); deploy MachineHealthCheck resources for automatic unhealthy node replacement; spread MachineSets across availability zones for high availability.

Unlimited scaling without resource quotas causes budget overruns; single availability zone deployment creates blast radius for zone failures; missing MachineHealthCheck leaves unhealthy nodes consuming capacity.

activities.description: Deploy ClusterResourceOverride operator and establish predictive capacity planning from historical metrics.

narratives.description: How to optimize predictive resource allocation

narrativeContexts.context: ClusterResourceOverride operator optimizes resource utilization by automatically adjusting request-to-limit ratios, while historical metrics analysis enables predictive capacity planning and proactive scaling adjustments.

Deploy ClusterResourceOverride operator with target utilization ratios; collect and analyze historical resource utilization data for capacity planning; configure cost optimization alerts for overprovisioned workloads; tune scaling policies based on application-specific traffic patterns; maintain multi-tenant resource isolation during dynamic scaling.

Aggressive overcommit ratios cause pod evictions during peak usage; predictive models based on insufficient historical data produce unreliable forecasts; ignoring cost attribution across tenants masks resource waste.

activities.name: Implement Graceful Degradation Patterns
activities.description: Implement circuit breakers, timeouts, retry logic, and graceful termination for failure handling.

narratives.name: Graceful Degradation
narratives.description: How to implement graceful degradation patterns

narrativeContexts.context: Graceful degradation patterns ensure applications handle failures without cascading outages, using circuit breakers, timeouts, retry logic with exponential backoff, rate limiting, and graceful SIGTERM termination.

Implement circuit breaker patterns for all external dependency calls; configure connection and request timeouts to prevent resource exhaustion; add retry logic with exponential backoff and jitter; implement rate limiting to protect against overload; configure preStop hooks for graceful SIGTERM handling to complete in-flight requests.

Missing circuit breakers allow cascading failures when dependencies go down; retry storms without backoff amplify load on degraded services; immediate pod termination without graceful shutdown drops active connections.

activities.description: Centralize application logs, Prometheus metrics, distributed traces, and configure SLO-based alerting.

narratives.name: Centralized Observability Setup
narratives.description: How to configure centralized observability

narrativeContexts.context: Centralized observability combines structured logging to stdout/stderr, Prometheus custom metrics endpoints, distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry, and SLO-based alerting into a unified view of application health.

Configure applications to log structured JSON to stdout/stderr for cluster logging collection; expose custom Prometheus metrics via ServiceMonitor resources; integrate distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry SDK; define custom alerts based on business-level SLOs; create Grafana dashboards correlating logs, metrics, and traces.

Unstructured logging prevents effective search and correlation; missing ServiceMonitor resources cause metrics gaps; alerting on symptoms without SLO context generates excessive noise without actionable information.

activities.name: Establish SRE Reliability Practices
activities.description: Define SLIs, SLOs, and error budgets; implement symptom-based alerting and systematic toil reduction.

narratives.name: SRE Reliability Practices
narratives.description: How to establish SRE reliability practices

narrativeContexts.context: SRE reliability practices establish measurable service level objectives, error budgets for data-driven reliability decisions, symptom-based alerting to reduce noise, systematic toil reduction, and chaos engineering to validate resilience assumptions.

Define Service Level Indicators (SLIs) reflecting customer experience (latency, availability, throughput); negotiate SLOs with stakeholders; implement error budget tracking and consumption transparency; replace cause-based alerts with symptom-based alerting tied to SLOs; identify and automate operational toil targeting below 50% of team capacity; introduce controlled chaos engineering experiments.

SLOs set without stakeholder agreement lack organizational commitment; cause-based alerting generates excessive false positives; neglecting toil measurement allows it to consume team capacity silently; chaos engineering without proper controls can cause real outages.

activities.name: Establish Baseline Image Security
activities.description: Configure trusted base image sources, enforce restricted SCC compliance, and integrate vulnerability scanning.

narratives.name: Baseline Image Security
narratives.description: How to establish baseline image security

narrativeContexts.context: Baseline image security establishes the foundational security posture by enforcing trusted Red Hat base images, restricted Security Context Constraint compliance, non-root execution, and initial vulnerability scanning integration.

Configure image pull policies to restrict base images to Red Hat or approved vendor repositories; verify all application Dockerfiles use non-root USER directives; test application compatibility with restricted SCC (the default in OpenShift); integrate basic image vulnerability scanning into CI pipeline; establish a process for tracking and applying base image security patches.

Applications that assume root access fail silently under restricted SCC; using unvetted community base images introduces unknown vulnerabilities; failing to update base images regularly leaves known CVEs unpatched.

activities.description: Implement SBOM generation, image signing with Trusted Artifact Signer, and cryptographic verification at admission.

narratives.name: Supply Chain Verification
narratives.description: How to verify software supply chain

narrativeContexts.context: Software supply chain verification uses cryptographic signing, SBOM generation, and provenance attestation to ensure only verified artifacts are deployed, leveraging Trusted Artifact Signer and Sigstore integration for end-to-end supply chain integrity.

Add SBOM generation tasks to Tekton pipelines using standard formats (SPDX or CycloneDX); integrate Trusted Artifact Signer for cosign-based image signing; configure ImagePolicy APIs to validate signatures at admission; enable continuous verification via transparency logs; protect AI/ML model deployments with Model Transparency Library.

Signing without admission-time verification provides false confidence; SBOM generation without consumption tooling creates compliance theater; signature key rotation without automation causes deployment failures.

narrativeContexts.context: Developer onboarding to OpenShift establishes the foundational experience through web console access with developer perspective, oc CLI configuration, and local development environments using Podman Desktop and Developer Sandbox.

Configure OAuth identity provider for SSO-based console authentication; enable the developer perspective in OpenShift console; distribute oc CLI installation guides and authentication procedures; provision Developer Sandbox access for no-cost experimentation; configure Podman Desktop for local container development and testing prior to cluster deployment.

Expecting developers to learn CLI before understanding concepts visually through the console slows adoption; not providing sandbox environments forces developers to learn on production clusters; insufficient documentation of authentication and CLI setup creates frustrating first experiences.

narratives.description: How to deploy cloud development environments

narrativeContexts.context: OpenShift Dev Spaces provides browser-based IDEs (VS Code, JetBrains) with remote compute, enabling consistent development environments that eliminate local setup friction and support nested container builds.

Deploy Dev Spaces operator with workspace template definitions; configure multi-workspace support with auto-pruner for etcd usage management; enable marketplace extensions for remote compute; set up nested container support for podman run capabilities within workspaces; connect Dev Spaces to source repositories and CI pipelines.

Insufficient workspace resource limits cause performance complaints; missing auto-pruner configuration leads to etcd bloat at scale; not supporting popular IDE extensions reduces developer willingness to adopt cloud environments.
